title: Mother Holle
paragraphs: Once upon a time there was a widow who had two daughters. One was beautiful and hard-working, the other ugly and lazy. But the mother loved the ugly, lazy one best, because she was her own daughter. So the other girl, who was only a stepdaughter, had to do all the housework and was treated just like Cinderella. Every day her stepmother sent her to sit by the well on the high road and spin until her fingers bled. Then one day it happened that some blood dropped onto the spindle, and as the girl bent over the well to wash it off, the spindle suddenly jumped out of her hand and fell into the well. She ran home in tears to tell about her misfortune, but her stepmother spoke harshly to her and, after giving her a fierce scolding, said coldly, “Since you let the spindle fall into the well, you can go and get it out yourself.”
Not knowing what else to do, the girl returned to the well, and in her despair she jumped into the water after the spindle.
The next thing she knew, she was waking up in a lovely meadow, bright with sunshine, where flowers by the thousand bloomed on every side.

She walked across the meadow, and soon she came to a baker’s oven full of bread, and the loaves called out to her, “Take us out, take us out, or we’ll burn to a cinder! We were baked through long ago.” So she took the bread shovel and pulled them all out.

Farther on she came to a tree loaded with apples. “Shake me, shake me, please,” the tree called out. “All my apples are ripe.” So she shook the tree, and the apples rained down on her. She kept shaking until not one apple was left on the branches. Then she stacked them neatly in a pile and went on her way.

The next thing she reached was a small house. An old woman was looking out of the window, and her teeth were so huge that the girl was terrified and started to run. But the old woman called after her, “Why are you afraid, dear child? Stay with me. If you do my housework properly, things will go very well for you. Just be sure to make my bed the right way: shake it hard, until the feathers fly. Down in the world, people say it is snowing when I do that, because I am Mother Holle.” She spoke so kindly that the girl found her courage and agreed to work for her.

She did everything exactly as the old woman asked, and each time she made the bed she shook it as hard as she could, so the feathers swirled around like snowflakes. The old woman kept her promise. She never raised her voice to the girl, and every day she served her roasted and boiled meat.

She stayed with Mother Holle for a good while, and then she grew unhappy. At first she could not say why she felt so low. Eventually she realized she was homesick, though she was a thousand times better off here than with her mother and sister. After a time she went to Mother Holle and said, “I miss home so much that I can’t stay with you any longer. I’m very happy here, but I have to go back to my own people.”
Mother Holle answered, “I’m glad you want to go back to your family. You have served me so faithfully and well that I will take you home myself.”

With that she took the girl by the hand and led her up to a wide gateway. The gate swung open, and as the girl walked through, a shower of gold poured down over her. The gold stuck to her, until she was covered in it from head to toe.
“This is your reward for working so hard,” said Mother Holle, and she gave her the spindle that had fallen into the well.
Then the gate closed, and the girl found herself back in the ordinary world, close to her mother’s house. As she came into the yard, the rooster sitting on the well crowed:

“Cock-a-doodle-doo!
Your golden daughter’s come back to you.”

She went in to her mother and sister, and since she was covered in gold, they welcomed her warmly. She told them everything that had happened to her. When the mother heard how she had come by such wealth, she wanted her own ugly, lazy daughter to go and try for the same luck. So she made that daughter sit by the well and spin. To get blood on her spindle, the girl pricked her finger and pushed her hand into a thorn-bush. Then she threw the spindle into the well and jumped in after it.

Like her sister, she woke up in the beautiful meadow and walked across it until she reached the oven. “Take us out, take us out, or we’ll burn to cinders! We were baked long ago,” cried the loaves, just as before. But the lazy girl answered, “Do you think I’m going to get my hands dirty for you?” and walked on.
Soon she came to the apple tree. “Shake me, shake me, please. All my apples are ripe,” it cried. But she only said, “What a thing to ask of me! An apple might fall on my head,” and went on.
At last she reached Mother Holle’s house. Her sister had told her all about the big teeth, so she was not afraid of them, and she hired herself out to the old woman right away.

On the first day she was obedient and hardworking, putting in great effort to please Mother Holle, because she was thinking of the gold she would get. On the second day she began to slack off, and on the third she was lazier still. After that she started lying in bed in the mornings and refusing to get up. Worse, she failed to make the old woman’s bed properly and forgot to shake it so that the feathers would fly. Before long Mother Holle was fed up with her and told her she could go. The lazy girl was delighted, and thought to herself, “The gold will soon be mine.” Mother Holle led her to the wide gateway, just as she had led her sister. But as the girl passed through, instead of a shower of gold, a huge bucketful of pitch poured down on her.
“That is what you have earned,” said the old woman, and she shut the gate.
So the lazy girl had to walk home covered in pitch, and when the rooster on the well saw her, he crowed:

“Cock-a-doodle-doo!
Your dirty daughter’s come back to you.”
No matter how she tried, she could not get the pitch off, and it stayed on her for the rest of her life.
